facts.text: James Dewar (1842–1923) grew up in Kincardine-on-Forth, Scotland.
Dewar studied at the University of Edinburgh and in 1875 became professor of experimental physics at Cambridge.
In 1887 Dewar became director of the Royal Institution in London.
Dewar worked on the science of extreme cold and succeeded in turning hydrogen gas into a liquid in 1898.
The Dewar flask is a double-walled glass container with a vacuum between the walls, coated with silver to cut heat flow by conduction and radiation.
In December 1892 Dewar showed his vacuum flask at a Friday evening lecture.
At that lecture Dewar broke the tip of one of his flasks holding liquid oxygen; air rushed into the vacuum space and the liquid oxygen began to boil wildly.
Because the two walls of a vacuum flask do not touch, heat cannot pass between them by conduction, except at the lip where they join.
With no air between the walls, heat cannot be carried across the gap by convection.
Shiny, reflective walls absorb very little heat radiation and, when warm, give off very little.
Cheap double-walled bottles filled with foam instead of a vacuum are not true Dewar flasks.
The Thermos vacuum bottle first went on sale for home and commercial use in Germany in May 1904.
In 1904 a German company named Thermos GmbH began commercial production of vacuum flasks.
In 1907 the Thermos trademark rights were sold to three companies: one in the United States, one in Canada and one in Britain.
In 1911 the British Thermos company produced the first machine-made glass inner bottle (filler).
A vacuum flask keeps its contents, from coffee to human tissue, hot or cold.
By 2004, four out of five Americans owned a Thermos.
A Thermos flask made in England in 1910–1920 had a silvered glass liner, a lid that worked as a cup and a cork stopper.
